# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven into how most organizations operate, that a good meeting is one where everyone leaves nodding. We celebrate alignment. We praise teams that "get on the same page." A meeting that ends in harmony feels productive; a meeting that ends in argument feels like a failure, or at least an unfinished piece of business.

But this assumption deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, can be deceptive. People nod along for many reasons that have nothing to do with genuine conviction: fatigue, deference to the most senior person in the room, the desire to end a meeting that has already run twenty minutes long, or simple reluctance to be the one voice of dissent. When a meeting ends with everyone agreeing, we may have achieved genuine consensus—or we may have merely swept uncertainty under the rug, where it will quietly shape decisions for weeks or months to come.
